title: The server is authoritative — the client only renders
content:
The client renders configuration and displays results. It never decides what is required, which fields are visible, or which stage transitions are legal.

Duplicating a rule client-side for responsiveness is fine. Treating the client's answer as truth is not — every gate is re-evaluated server-side from the same configuration rows.

lib/api/client.ts is the only module that calls the API. Components never fetch.

lib/api/generated/ is build output from openapi-typescript. Regenerate it; never hand-edit it.

features/ never imports from another feature. Shared code moves to components/ui/ or lib/.

Public routes must render meaningful HTML without JavaScript — that is the entire reason SSR was chosen.

See docs/codebase-structure.md §15.

title: Work in a worktree per task
content:
Create a git worktree for each task so parallel agents do not collide in the same working directory:

    git worktree add ../sebp-<task-slug> -b <task-slug>

Branch name matches the task slug. .pad.toml is committed, so the worktree resolves the same Pad workspace automatically — shared task state, isolated filesystem.

Claim the task atomically before starting:

    pad item update TASK-N --status in-progress --expected-updated-at <updated_at you read>

A non-zero exit means another agent claimed it first. Pick a different task rather than forcing the update.

Pad coordinates the work; git isolates the code. You need both — Pad will happily report two agents progressing on tasks that are overwriting each other's files.

title: Independent AI code review before merge
content:
Have an independent AI reviewer look at the changes before merge, using a DIFFERENT model than the one that implemented them. Reviewing with the same model that wrote the code is closer to self-review.

Implementation here is done with Claude, so review runs through codex (installed on this machine). The loop is: request review, address every finding, re-review until clean.

Before requesting review, review your own diff first — debug code left behind, missing error handling, unclear names, unintended changes.

Also confirm the mechanical gates pass: pnpm lint && pnpm depcruise && pnpm test, with 100% coverage. Do not open a PR expecting review to catch what CI would have.

title: Failures are Result values, not exceptions
content:
domain/ and use-cases/ return Result<T, E>. Error kinds are discriminated unions owned by the module. throw is reserved for programmer error — a thrown error is a 500 and a bug report.

The HTTP layer maps error kinds to status codes in one place (http/middleware/error.ts), never scattered through routes.

This exists because of the 100% coverage gate: every failure must be reachable and assertable from an HTTP test. Exceptions create catch blocks, and catch blocks are the branches hardest to cover from outside.

Corollary — do not write defensive guards for states the type system already prevents. If a branch cannot be reached by any request, it is dead code. Delete it, or change the types so the state is unrepresentable. A PR that lowers a coverage threshold is not a fix.

See docs/codebase-structure.md §8.

title: Anything replaceable goes behind a port
content:
Infrastructure is reached through interfaces the domain owns, never directly. This includes things we have no current intention of changing — the point is that the decision stays cheap.

Ports today: Clock, IdGenerator, ObjectStorage (R2), KeyValueStore (KV), JobQueue (Queues), Notifier (Pingram), plus each module's repositories and queries.

The test for whether something needs a port: if replacing it would mean editing files outside adapters/ and platform/, it needs one.

Ports are named for the capability (ObjectStorage, Notifier). Adapters are named for the technology (R2ObjectStorage, PingramNotifier). Never the reverse.

Adapters are constructed only in container.ts. Not in a route, not in a use-case, not in a test helper. Modules receive ports, never the container itself — passing the container is service-locator and defeats the point.

One exception exists: better-auth. It owns its own schema and middleware and is not wrapped, but its reach is confined to modules/identity and http/middleware/auth.ts. Every other module sees a branded UserId.

See docs/codebase-structure.md §6 and §7.

title: Tests go through HTTP with real infrastructure
Nothing is hardcoded — stages, fields and documents are data
content:
Stages, per-stage fields, and document requirements are rows in the database, edited by admins at runtime. They are never constants in source code.

If you find yourself writing any of these, stop — it belongs in configuration:

    const STAGES = ['applied', 'screening', 'interview']   // forbidden
    if (stage.key === 'interview') { ... }                 // forbidden
    requiredDocs = ['pitch_deck', 'incorporation_cert']    // forbidden

This is not a style preference. Runtime-configurable stages, fields, and documents are the product — a hardcoded stage list silently destroys the reason sebp exists, and it will not be caught by tests, because the tests will have been written against the same hardcoded list.

The only sanctioned switch on a field's data type is the validator factory in the API and the renderer map in the frontend. Everywhere else, behaviour is driven by configuration rows.

See docs/technical-design.md §1.1 and §5.

title: Respect module boundaries — import barrels, never internals
content:
A module's index.ts is its entire public surface: domain types, port interfaces, and a factory. Everything else is private.

From outside a module, the only legal import path is `@/modules/<name>`. Any deeper path is a dependency-cruiser error, not a review comment.

    import type { Application } from '@/modules/application'                    // yes
    import { D1ApplicationRepo } from '@/modules/application/adapters/d1/...'   // no
    import { evaluateGate } from '@/modules/application/domain/transition'      // no

When one module needs behaviour from another, depend on the other module's port and let the composition root inject the implementation. If two modules need each other's internals, the boundary is drawn in the wrong place — move the code rather than widening the surface.

See docs/codebase-structure.md §4.

title: Domain stays pure — no framework, no I/O, no clock
content:
domain/ imports no Hono, no Drizzle, no Zod, no cloudflare:workers, and no better-auth. It performs no I/O. It is pure functions and entities.

Banned in domain/ and use-cases/: Date.now(), new Date(), Math.random(), crypto.randomUUID(). Take a Clock or IdGenerator port as an argument instead — otherwise the behaviour is untestable and time-dependent.

Repositories return domain entities, not database rows. A Drizzle row type must never escape adapters/; mapping happens there and nowhere else.

This is what makes the D1-to-Postgres escape hatch in ADR 0001 a genuine option rather than a comforting sentence. Every leak makes the swap more expensive.

See docs/codebase-structure.md §5.

title: Run tests before completing tasks
content:
Run `pnpm test` (Vitest with `@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers`) before marking any task done. If tests fail, fix them before completing the task — do not mark a task done with a red suite and a note to fix it later.

Both repositories use the same command. Run it in the repo you changed; if a change spans the API and the frontend, run both.

Until a repository actually has a test suite, the requirement is to manually verify the change works end to end and say in the task comment what you verified. "It compiles" is not verification.

title: Conventional commit format
content: Use conventional commit format for all commit messages: feat:, fix:, docs:, refactor:, test:, chore:. Include scope when relevant, e.g. feat(api): add user endpoint

title: Never push directly to main
content: Never commit or push directly to the main/master branch. Always use feature branches and merge via pull request.

title: Review your own changes before PR
content: Before creating a PR, review your own diff. Check for: debug code left behind, missing error handling, unclear variable names, and unintended changes.
